topic.name: Sums of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Parametric Curves

question.text: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_C -\dfrac{1}{z}\,\mathrm{d}x + {x}\,\mathrm{d}y + \mathrm{d}z,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + t\,\mathbf{j} + \sin t\,\mathbf{k}$ for $ t\in\left[0,\pi\right]. $
question.explanation:
Along the curve, we have \[ x(t) = \cos t, \qquad y(t) = t, \qquad z(t)=\sin t. \]

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\mathbf{k}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( \cos t \right) \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( t \right) \, \mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( \sin t \right)\, \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= -\sin t\,\mathbf{i} + \,\mathbf{j} + \cos t\,\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_C -\dfrac{1}{z}\,\mathrm{d}x + {x}\,\mathrm{d}y + \mathrm{d}z &= \int_0^{\pi} -\dfrac{1}{z} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \,\mathrm{d}t + x \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \,\mathrm{d}t + \dfrac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] &= \int_0^{\pi} \left( -\dfrac{1}{z} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} + x \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} + \dfrac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \right) \mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = \int_0^{\pi} -\dfrac{1}{\sin{t}} \cdot (-\sin{t}) + {\cos{t}} \cdot 1 + \cos{t} \, \textrm d t\\[5pt] & = \int_0^{\pi} 1 + 2\cos{t} \, \textrm d t\\[5pt] &= (t + 2\sin{t} ) \, \bigg|_0^{\pi}\\[5pt] &= \pi + 2\sin{\pi} - 0 \\[5pt] &= \pi \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + x\,\mathrm{d}y,$ where $C$ is a portion of the parabola parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)= 2t\,\mathbf{i} + (2-t^2)\,\mathbf{j}$ for $ t\in[0,1]. $
question.explanation:
Along the curve, we have \[ x(t) = 2t, \qquad y(t) =2-t^2. \]

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( 2t \right) \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( 2-t^2 \right) \, \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= 2\,\mathbf{i} -2t\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_C (x+y)\,\mathrm{d}x +x\,\mathrm{d}y &=\int_0^{1} (x+y) \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\,\mathrm{d}t + x \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{1} \left[ (x+y) \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + x \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \right] \mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{1} (2t+2-t^2)\cdot 2 + 2t\cdot (-2t)\,\textrm d t\\[5pt] &= \int_0^{1} -6t^2 +4t +4 \:\textrm d t\\[5pt] &= \left[ -2t^3 + 2t^2 + 4t \right]_0^{1} \\[5pt] &= (-2+2+4) - 0 \\[5pt] &= 4 \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C y^2\,\mathrm{d}x + x\,\mathrm{d}y + z\,\mathrm{d}z,$ where $C$ is a portion of the line $\mathbf{r}(t)=t\,\mathbf{i} + 2t\,\mathbf{j} + 3t\,\mathbf{k}$ for $ t\in[0,5]?$
question.explanation:
Along the curve, we have \[ x(t) = t, \qquad y(t) = 2t, \qquad z(t) = 3t. \]

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\mathbf{k}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( t\right) \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( 2t\right) \, \mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( 3t \right)\, \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \,\mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j} +3\, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_C y^2\,\mathrm{d}x + x\,\mathrm{d}y + z\,\mathrm{d}z &=\int_0^{5} y^2 \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \,\mathrm{d}t + x \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \,\mathrm{d}t + z \dfrac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{5} \left( y^2 \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} + x \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} + z \dfrac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \right) \mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] &=\int_0^{5} 4t^2 \cdot (1) + t \cdot (2) + 3t \cdot (3)\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{5} 4t^2+11t \,\mathrm{d}t %&=\int_0^{5} \cos 2t + t^2\,\mathrm{d}t \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C xy\,\mathrm{d}x + y\,\mathrm{d}y + z\,\mathrm{d}z,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=t\,\mathbf{i} + t^2\,\mathbf{j} + t^3\,\mathbf{k}$ for $ t\in[3,5]?$
question.explanation:
Along the curve, we have \[ x(t) = t, \qquad y(t) = t^2, \qquad z(t) = t^3. \]

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\mathbf{k}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( t\right) \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( t^2\right) \, \mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( t^3\right)\, \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \,\mathbf{i} + 2t\,\mathbf{j} + 3t^2\,\mathbf{j} . \end{align*}

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_C xy\,\mathrm{d}x + y\,\mathrm{d}y + z\,\mathrm{d}z &=\int_3^{5} xy \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \,\mathrm{d}t + y \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \,\mathrm{d}t + z \dfrac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=\int_3^{5} \left( xy \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} + y \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} + z \dfrac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \right) \mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] &=\int_3^{5} t^3 \cdot (1) + t^2 \cdot (2t) + t^3 \cdot (3t^2)\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=\int_3^{5} 3t^5+3t^3 \,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=3\int_3^{5} t^5+t^3 \,\mathrm{d}t \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + y\,\mathrm{d}y,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = (\cos t+1)\,\mathbf{i} + (\sin t -1)\,\mathbf{j}$ for $ t\in\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]?$
question.explanation:
Along the curve, we have \[ x(t) = \cos t + 1, \qquad y(t) = \sin t - 1. \]

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\,\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\cos t+1)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\sin t-1) \,\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= -\sin t \,\mathbf{i} + \cos t \,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_C (x+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + y\,\mathrm{d}y & = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} (x+y)\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\,\mathrm{d}t + y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \left((x+y)\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} (\cos t +1 + \sin t - 1)\cdot (-\sin t) + (\sin t - 1) \cdot \cos t \:\textrm d t \\[5pt] &=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} -\cos t\sin t - \sin^2 t + \sin t\cos t - \cos t \:\textrm d t \\[5pt] &=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} -\sin^2 t - \cos t \:\textrm d t \end{align*}
